title: Spielberg Ditched Harry Potter to Honor Kubrick—and Gave Us a Sci-Fi Cult Classic
summary: In the late 1990s, the world was gripped by Pottermania, and Steven Spielberg was set to direct the first film adaptation. But he walked away, and now we know exactly why: a promise to his old friend Stanley Kubrick. Speaking with TCM to promote his new alien film Disclosure Day, Spielberg recounted how, at Kubrick's funeral, the director's widow Christiane and her brother Jan Harlan approached him. They asked him to take over Kubrick's long-gestating project, A.I. Artificial Intelligence. "I actually walked away from Harry Potter, which I was scheduled to direct as my next movie," Spielberg said. "I gave it up. It was going to be a huge movie because the book already was a runaway cultural phenomenon. I gave that up to essentially do A.I." The revelation is startling because Spielberg was further along on Harry Potter than previously known. He had a script and was deep in pre-production. But the pull of Kubrick's vision was stronger. A.I., which opened in June 2001—just five months before Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone—tells the story of David, a robotic boy programmed to love, in a bleak future world. It's a film that split critics and audiences, blending Kubrick's chilly intellect with Spielberg's emotional warmth. Over time, it's become a cult classic, praised for its ambition and unsettling questions about humanity. Spielberg's choice had ripple effects. Chris Columbus stepped in to direct Harry Potter, launching a franchise that defined a generation. Meanwhile, Spielberg embarked on a run of deeply personal, sometimes strange films: Minority Report, Catch Me If You Can, Munich. He told TCM he has no regrets. For fans of weird, wonderful cinema, that's a win. As one critic put it, you couldn't ask for two movies more worlds apart—and we're lucky to have both.
why_it_matters: Spielberg's choice shows how creative loyalty and personal connections can shape entire entertainment landscapes—both Harry Potter and A.I. exist because one director honored a friend, and that outcome brings us two very different worlds to enjoy.

background_read: Stanley Kubrick (director of 2001: A Space Odyssey and The Shining) had been working on A.I. since the 1970s before his death in 1999.
Steven Spielberg (director of Jaws, E.T., and Jurassic Park) was a close friend who often discussed the project with Kubrick over the years.
At the time, the Harry Potter book series by J.K. Rowling was a worldwide literary phenomenon, and the film adaptation was one of the most anticipated movies ever.
Jan Harlan, a producer and Kubrick's brother-in-law, helped coordinate the handoff of A.I. to Spielberg, knowing Spielberg would respect Kubrick's vision.
Chris Columbus, known for directing family films like Home Alone, stepped in and shaped the Harry Potter franchise into a massive success that defined a generation.

perspectives.description: Spielberg fulfilled a promise to a legendary friend, and his take on A.I. became a thoughtful, unique film. Fans of both franchises can appreciate two distinct works that might never have existed otherwise.

Harry Potter under Spielberg could have been visually groundbreaking and more cinematic; some feel the series ended up too safe. Additionally, A.I. was a commercial disappointment and confused audiences with its mixed tone.

This story illustrates how film industry decisions get driven by personal debts and timing rather than purely business logic. Cult classics often emerge precisely because a director took a risk that mainstream producers would avoid.

As streaming and AI change filmmaking, directors may face similar crossroads between blockbuster franchises and personal art. The legacy of this choice might inspire future filmmakers to honor mentors even at the cost of huge paychecks.
